q: What makes this a gradation even though panel size stays constant?
o: A visual property changes through successive degrees across the sequence.
Every panel has an unrelated colour without an ordered relationship.
Equal panel dimensions make the colour progression irrelevant to composition.
Only an increase in physical height can establish gradation.
n: Gradation is progressive change, not exclusively a change in dimensions. Colour intensity or value can vary through successive degrees while panel geometry remains constant. The organizing feature is the readable progression. An arbitrary collection of different colours would provide variety but would not necessarily establish gradation.

q: What evidence best supports describing its form as functionally derived?
o: The systems share a consistent visual language, even if their placement reduces useful space.
The arrangement improves usable exhibition space and supports actual systems and movement.
The exterior is recognizable, even if its organization complicates the intended activities.
The exterior resembles a familiar industrial style regardless of its interior operation.
ref: Zoom lecture 03:07:50–03:14:58; Centre Pompidou — An iconic architecture: https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/centre-pompidou-is-transforming-itself/an-iconic-architecture
n: The Centre Pompidou discussion connects the visible building to functional consequences: flexibility, services distribution and movement. Functional expression requires that the arrangement actually serves those needs. Decorative imitation does not establish the same relationship. The precedent illustrates a strategy to evaluate, not a rule that all buildings should expose their services.

q: Which trade-off should the designer evaluate?
o: Exposure alone, assuming every service must be outside to be functional.
The service colour alone, assuming colour coding resolves physical access.
The desired enclosure and appearance against access, disruption and the space needed by services.
Appearance alone, because maintenance begins after architectural design has ended.
ref: Zoom lecture 03:07:50–03:14:30; Centre Pompidou — An iconic architecture: https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/centre-pompidou-is-transforming-itself/an-iconic-architecture
n: The lecture notes that services consume space and can make maintenance disruptive when access is poorly considered. Their treatment should account for both the architectural enclosure and future access. Exposing every system is not a universal answer; the useful design lesson is to consider these physical and operational consequences together.

q: What is the most appropriate design response?
o: Reduce the furniture provision before checking which activities require it.
Retain the furniture arrangement and ask users to adapt their routes around it.
Reassess furniture and movement clearances using the intended users and activities.
Accept the layout because the minimum area alone proves its usability.
n: Minimum compliance and practical usability are different evaluations. The lecture uses sofa-to-table spacing to show why body dimensions and activities inform planning beyond a general minimum. The response should investigate the layout and clearance problem directly. Material appearance or lighting may affect experience but does not remove the stated obstruction.

q: What should guide the choice of dimensional evidence?
o: The assumption that all published body measurements are interchangeable.
The relevance of the measured population and activities to the people expected to use the seating.
The reference with the most familiar drawing style, irrespective of its users.
The reference that provides the smallest dimensions and therefore the most seats.
n: The lecture recommends dimensional information relevant to the intended population. A reference is useful because its measurements relate to actual users and activities, not merely because it is available. The recording does not establish a numerical percentile method, so the question tests appropriate evidence selection without inventing dimension standards.

q: Which description best matches the lecture’s scope of environmental design?
o: Evaluating the architecture mainly through its exterior visual composition.
Designing planted areas independently of the surrounding built systems.
Selecting ecological products after the buildings and streets have been fixed.
Coordinating the physical environment across related design disciplines.
n: Environmental design is used broadly in the lecture: architecture, engineering, landscape, urban design and planning contribute to one physical setting. Treating it only as planting or product selection misses the relationships among those systems. This scope explains why a building decision may need coordination beyond the building itself.

q: What coordination task remains?
o: Let both designers issue separate junctions without comparing them.
Wait for installation before deciding which materials and levels must meet.
Treat the label as proof that the architectural interface needs no further attention.
Agree who develops the junction and reconcile the adjoining design information.
n: Assigning a package to another designer identifies responsibility but does not resolve the physical interface. The lecture stresses exchanging information and coordinating junctions so separately developed work fits together. A note identifying another consultant should direct the reader to coherent information rather than leave a gap between the packages.

q: At which design focus is this investigation most directly operating?
o: Object styling: the appearance of one building considered separately.
Component detailing: the assembly of a particular façade joint.
Interior space planning: the arrangement of furnishings within a room.
Urban design: the physical relationships of urban buildings and spaces.
n: Urban design examines relationships among urban structures and spaces. The scale and subject here go beyond one isolated building or interior: frontages, routes and squares form a connected setting. The lecture introduces this relationship to city planning without supplying a complete urban-design method or a regulatory classification for every project.

q: Which first diagram most faithfully represents the available information?
o: Draw a final buildable envelope from the stated access-road location alone.
Use familiar setback values without annotation to complete the initial drawing.
Show the described buildings and road; label setback requirements as unresolved.
Omit the existing buildings until the new building’s preferred form is selected.
n: The first representation should distinguish known conditions from assumptions. Invented setbacks can make an unverified envelope look authoritative, while omitting existing buildings changes the problem. An unresolved constraint should be investigated and clearly identified. The lecture links inaccurate visualization with recommendations that solve a different spatial problem.

q: What is the most useful correction?
o: Examine the repeated rooms and major hall now because principles also organize plans.
Replace the plan analysis with a material palette to establish the principles.
Give every room an identical role so that principles need not affect the plan.
Complete the elevations first because plans cannot express compositional relationships.
n: The lecture applies principles to façades, plans and larger arrangements. Repeated rooms can establish rhythm, while a major hall can establish hierarchy before any exterior treatment is chosen. Reviewing these relationships early connects composition to use and organization rather than treating principles as decoration added to an already fixed layout.

q: Which comment best uses the lecture’s shared language of design?
o: The heavy roof mass makes the slender supports appear poorly proportioned.
The façade should remain unchanged because aesthetic judgments cannot be discussed.
The façade is unsuccessful because this is not my preferred architectural style.
The scheme must be beautiful because its designer used mathematical proportions.
n: A useful critique identifies a relationship the team can examine and revise. Roof-to-support proportion is more actionable than a statement of taste. Shared principles support reasoned discussion, but they do not guarantee universal agreement or beauty. The lecture’s subjective/objective distinction is best used as a distinction between preference and explicit compositional reasoning.

q: Which representation best supports this stage of work?
o: Simple relationship diagrams that make alternatives quick to compare and revise.
One photorealistic exterior image concealing the unresolved adjacencies.
A detailed specification of fittings before the relationships are compared.
Fully dimensioned construction plans with every wall finish resolved.
n: Early diagrams let a designer revise spatial relationships with limited investment in details that may change. Their value here is the speed and clarity of comparison, not precision about construction. Premature detail can consume time and create attachment to a weak option without establishing whether its basic arrangement satisfies the programme.

q: Which principle is the focus of this evaluation?
o: Unity: whether the parts contribute to a coherent overall intent.
Gradation: whether each successive element grows by a regular increment.
Anomaly: whether one element departs from an established pattern.
Bilateral symmetry: whether both halves match across a single axis.
n: Unity concerns the coherence of the whole, not only identical elements. The proposed tower is being tested for its relationship to the pavilion’s governing idea. Rhythm, balance and harmony may contribute, but the question specifically asks whether the overall concept remains intact. An addition is not inherently wrong; its integration must be evaluated.

q: Which statement best evaluates its potential unity?
o: The differences can support unity when they contribute to the shared organizing intent.
Different room sizes prevent unity even when the overall sequence is coherent.
A coherent sequence establishes that every individual design decision is already successful.
Unity depends primarily on replacing all materials with one uniform finish.
n: Unity does not require literal sameness. Varied components can contribute to one intelligible purpose, such as a sequence of increasingly quiet spaces. That relationship should still be tested in detail; identifying a concept is not proof that all decisions support it. Uniform materials alone cannot repair an incoherent spatial arrangement.

q: Which conclusion is justified from this description?
o: The arrangement may demonstrate asymmetrical visual balance.
The arrangement demonstrates bilateral symmetry across the entrance axis.
The arrangement proves that its structural forces are in equilibrium.
The arrangement must be unbalanced because its masses are unequal.
n: Visual balance can result from relationships among unlike parts. Identical masses are not necessary for a settled composition, and unequal parts do not form a mirror merely because they balance perceptually. This visual judgment also cannot substitute for structural analysis. The lecture distinguishes symmetrical examples from an asymmetrical composition at Walt Disney Concert Hall.

q: Which compositional issue should be investigated?
o: The main entrance is sufficiently legible because its intended role appears in the programme.
The use of more than one emphasis device prevents either entrance from attracting attention.
Several emphasis devices may be assigning visual priority to the wrong entrance.
Entrance prominence is determined only by floor area, regardless of colour or location.
n: Height, colour, exposure and other differences can reinforce one another in attracting attention. If those cues favour a secondary entrance, the visible hierarchy may contradict the intended route. The designer should connect emphasis to the actual priority of destinations rather than assume that the written programme communicates itself to visitors.

q: Which explanation best captures the lecture’s counterpoint reading?
o: The new entrance eliminates contrast by using a completely different material.
Difference remains visible while participating in a larger compositional dialogue.
The new entrance succeeds only because it duplicates the historic façades.
The surrounding complex is irrelevant once the entrance becomes prominent.
ref: Zoom lecture 02:59:03–03:02:55; Musée du Louvre — A pyramid for a symbol: https://www.louvre.fr/en/explore/the-palace/a-pyramid-for-a-symbol
n: Counterpoint retains a relationship between contrasting parts. In the Louvre discussion, the instructor moves beyond noticing dissimilar materials to considering how the intervention relates to its setting. The Louvre confirms respect for the palace layout and transparency. Copying the old architecture is not required, and prominence alone does not explain contextual compatibility.

q: Which articulation most directly reinforces that intent?
o: Closely spaced horizontal bands that visually divide the height into short layers.
An unstructured mix of competing directions without a dominant relationship.
A single isolated change in colour with no connection to the directional composition.
A repeated sequence whose dominant continuous direction is vertical.
n: Repeated features may reinforce or counter a building’s dominant direction. Vertical continuity can emphasize ascent, whereas repeated horizontal divisions may moderate it. The important step is to connect the direction of repetition to the intended reading; rhythm does not have one fixed directional effect in every design.

q: Which feature distinguishes gradation in panel B from the regular rhythm in panel A?
o: The elements establish an equal mirrored pair across a centre.
The repeated elements change progressively in height.
The elements have been arranged without any common relationship.
The elements stop repeating as soon as their sizes differ.
n: Gradation is a systematic change through successive degrees, such as increasing height. It can work within a rhythmic sequence; rhythm does not require every unit to be identical. Panel A uses repetition of similar units, while panel B adds a progressive change. Neither arrangement establishes structural capacity or a required building proportion.

q: Which functional concern is highlighted by the Pompidou discussion?
o: The number of supports matters only to the façade composition.
A regular support grid guarantees that every exhibition arrangement will fit.
Fixed internal obstructions can limit the flexibility of display and partition arrangements.
An expressive exterior compensates for restrictions in usable exhibition space.
ref: Zoom lecture 03:07:50–03:14:30; Centre Pompidou — An iconic architecture: https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/centre-pompidou-is-transforming-itself/an-iconic-architecture
n: The lecture links structural placement to the flexibility of exhibition areas. Supports within the usable floor can constrain displays and partitions, so their arrangement belongs in the design discussion. This does not prescribe one structural solution for every gallery; it identifies the functional consequence that alternative systems should be evaluated against.

q: Which distinction best explains the two activities?
o: Anthropometry determines all psychological and organizational aspects of the task.
Measurement is ergonomics; adjusting a task is exclusively a study of visual proportion.
Measurement supplies anthropometric data; task-based adjustment applies ergonomic reasoning.
Both activities are completed solely by checking the room’s minimum legal floor area.
ref: Zoom lecture 03:15:00–03:19:59; International Ergonomics Association — What is ergonomics?: https://iea.cc/about/what-is-ergonomics/
n: Anthropometry concerns body dimensions; ergonomics uses human knowledge to improve interaction with tasks and systems. The lecture’s data/application distinction helps separate measurement from design use. Ergonomics is broader than body measurements alone, so testing the actual activity matters. Compliance with a room-area minimum cannot answer all workstation questions.

q: What should the comparison establish?
o: Whether the new route preserves accessible destinations and improves the intended usable floor arrangement.
Whether moving the route to the edge makes its function irrelevant to the plan.
Whether the exterior silhouette becomes unusual, regardless of circulation performance.
Whether an edge route can be selected without checking entrances or destinations.
ref: Zoom lecture 03:07:50–03:14:30; Centre Pompidou — An iconic architecture: https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/centre-pompidou-is-transforming-itself/an-iconic-architecture
n: The Pompidou example connects visible circulation to the organization of usable interior space. Relocation is valuable only if movement and destination access still work while the floor arrangement improves. The lesson is not that external or peripheral routes always succeed, but that circulation placement changes both spatial continuity and operational performance.

q: Which action best protects the intended design?
o: Resolve the design responsibility and issue coordinated, consistent finish information.
Let the contractor choose whichever specification is cheaper without clarification.
Keep both specifications because separate disciplines may contradict one another.
Delete every lobby reference from the architectural set without checking interfaces.
n: The lecture warns that conflicting consultant information can reach procurement or construction. Clear responsibility and coordinated documents prevent parallel instructions from creating a different built result. Referencing another consultant’s scope is useful, but physical interfaces still require coordination. Neither an undocumented contractor choice nor deletion of all related information resolves the design question.

q: Why is seat height alone an incomplete evaluation?
o: Arm support matters only when the room exceeds a particular floor area.
Reach difficulties should be addressed only by changing the chair’s visual style.
A suitable seat height establishes that every workstation relationship is also suitable.
Posture and use depend on the relationships among chair, supports, reach and work surface.
n: The chair example extends beyond a single measurement to posture, backrest, arms and the work surface. Ergonomic evaluation considers those interactions during the task. A component can have an individually reasonable dimension while its relationship to other components makes the complete workstation awkward or difficult to use.

q: Which sequence completes the planning logic described in the lecture?
o: Assess present conditions, forecast future requirements, then plan how to meet them.
Reproduce the present arrangement, then forecast demand after construction.
Forecast future requirements, then disregard existing conditions to avoid constraints.
Select a preferred future image, then collect only data that supports it.
n: The lecture connects an appraisal of the present with anticipated requirements and a response to those requirements. Existing conditions provide a starting point, not a permanent template. A plan that merely preserves today’s arrangement may fail to address future needs; a forecast disconnected from existing conditions can be equally weak.

q: What is the strongest basis for recommending a finish?
o: Choose the finish used in the largest number of the architect’s previous projects.
Prioritize appearance now and leave maintenance evaluation to the operator.
Compare whole-project requirements, durability and maintenance within the budget.
Choose the higher initial price as the clearest indicator of long-term suitability.
n: A recommendation is defensible when it responds to the actual brief. The lecture’s finish example makes “best” dependent on criteria rather than familiarity or price alone. Comparing durability, maintenance and budget reveals the trade-offs; similar appearance does not mean similar suitability. The brief must identify which requirements are essential.

q: What does this disagreement show?
o: The stronger personal preference is sufficient to establish a universal judgment.
Agreement about proportions establishes that both reviewers must like the style.
Shared compositional observations can coexist with different personal preferences.
Different preferences prevent either reviewer from discussing the composition.
n: The lecture distinguishes personal taste from reasoning that other people can inspect. Recognizing a proportion or pattern does not compel identical preferences. Aesthetic discussion becomes more useful when participants identify both the observable relationship and the value they assign to it, without presenting personal liking as a universal result.

q: What should the next planning step preserve?
o: The exact circular outlines as the required geometry of every finished room.
The diagram’s spacing as the final thickness of walls and service zones.
The agreed functional connections while testing dimensions and circulation.
The apparent size of each bubble as a verified area requirement in square metres.
n: A bubble diagram represents relationships at an early level of resolution. Development must test whether real room dimensions, circulation and construction can preserve those relationships. Bubble shape and spacing are not automatically room geometry or measured clearance. This is why diagrams help exploration but still need development into workable plans.

q: Why is this still a space-planning task?
o: Space planning includes arranging and furnishing spaces in existing as well as proposed buildings.
Furniture decisions become space planning only when they change the structural system.
An existing shell makes all remaining decisions matters of surface appearance.
Space planning applies only when a new external building form is being designed.
n: The lecture’s definition includes proposed and existing spaces. Rearranging activities and furnishings changes how people use and move through a building, even when the shell stays in place. The relevant test is whether the work addresses spatial relationships and use, rather than whether it produces a new building exterior.

q: What should precede fixing the building envelope?
o: Confirm adopted requirements and effective dates with the relevant local authority.
Defer the zoning check until detailed construction drawings have been completed.
Assume the saved plan remains applicable throughout the entire design commission.
Treat the announced amendment as already effective without checking its status.
n: The lecture’s due-diligence example shows how outdated planning assumptions can cause redesign. The useful task is to establish what applies to this property and application, including effective dates and transition issues. A future proposal and an adopted requirement are different. Neither the oldest saved file nor the newest announcement is automatically the governing document.

s: Testing a part against the whole
q: Which critique most directly tests unity?
o: Assess its material independently and leave its relationship to the building unexamined.
Approve it because an attractive component necessarily improves the complete building.
Compare whether adding the canopy strengthens or weakens the organizing idea of the whole.
Reject it because unity requires every component to have exactly the same dimensions.
n: The lecture proposes adding, removing or changing a part as a way to test its contribution to the whole. Unity concerns that contribution, rather than the isolated quality of the part. A new component may succeed through a compatible variation, but it should be evaluated against the established organizing idea.

q: Which interpretation most directly describes the relationship among these different materials?
o: Harmony through compatible variety.
Anomaly through disruption of a repeated field.
Symmetry through mirrored material placement.
Gradation through incremental enlargement.
n: Harmony explains how different elements can work together without clashing. Identical material is not required. Here the stated evidence concerns compatibility of varied textures and materials, not a progressive sequence, mirrored arrangement or interruption of a norm. The lecture applies this reasoning to both a contemporary house and the relationship of Fallingwater to its setting.

q: What should a critique examine to assess harmony with the setting?
o: How material, direction and level relationships allow built and natural elements to work together.
Whether all constructed elements disappear from every viewpoint.
Whether the house copies every visible rock outline exactly.
Whether all parts use the same texture regardless of their spatial role.
n: The Fallingwater discussion combines material contrast, horizontal and vertical elements, and relationships to the landscape. Harmony here involves compatible differences rather than literal imitation or invisibility. The rough and smooth parts can remain distinct while supporting a coherent relationship between construction and the natural setting.

q: What makes anomaly the most precise explanation of the emphasis in panel B?
o: The composition depends on matching every element across a central axis.
The darker tone creates emphasis without requiring a repeated pattern.
Every element uses a different form, leaving no common order to interrupt.
A distinct element interrupts an already legible repeated order.
n: Anomaly depends on an expectation established by the surrounding order. The repeated squares provide that expectation and the circle departs from it. Contrast is also present, but the question focuses on disruption of a pattern. Structural strength and symmetry are different issues that cannot be inferred from the diagram.

q: Which term is most directly supported by the given evidence?
o: Symmetry, because the surfaces are next to one another.
Gradation, because the pair establishes a sequence of incremental changes.
Anomaly, because any pair of dissimilar materials establishes a broken repeated order.
Contrast, because the comparison identifies dissimilar properties.
n: Contrast can be identified from a direct comparison of different properties. Anomaly requires an established order or expectation from which something departs; that evidence is not supplied here. The distinction matters because the same object can support different analyses depending on whether the question examines a pair or a broader patterned context.

q: Which compositional change most directly applies the lecture’s rhythm example?
o: Enlarge a single window without relating it to any repeated sequence.
Introduce a considered sequence of vertical bays along its length.
Change the building’s colour while leaving all articulation unchanged.
Remove all vertical divisions and strengthen continuous horizontal bands.
n: Repeated vertical articulation can break the reading of an extended horizontal façade into a sequence. Continuous horizontal bands would tend to reinforce the direction the brief wants to moderate. A single larger opening may create emphasis, but does not by itself establish rhythm. The effect should be evaluated against the intended composition.
